## Research question

Is kukui carbon-isotope composition associated with elevation, and what does rainfall add to the interpretation of that relationship?

## Case study

Lincoln, Noa Kekuewa, Mark D. McCoy, and Thegn N. Ladefoged. 2018. Stable Carbon and Nitrogen Isotopes in Kukui (*Aleurites moluccanus*) Endocarp along Rainfall and Elevation Gradients: Archaeological Implications. *PLOS ONE* 13(10): e0204654. [Read the case study](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0204654).

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

data_path <- if (file.exists("data/kukui_sites.csv")) {
  "data/kukui_sites.csv"
} else {
  "assignments/assignment09_kukui_correlation/data/kukui_sites.csv"
}

dat <- read_csv(data_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(dat)
```

The teaching file contains **71 sampled sites on Hawaiʻi Island**. One observation is one site record. The isotope values summarize multiple fruits from each site.

Elevation (m) is the main variable compared with kukui carbon-isotope composition (δ¹³C, in ‰). Annual rainfall (mm/year) is a second environmental variable used to explore the association.

## 4. Interpretation

Explain why the elevation–δ13C correlation does not by itself establish a causal mechanism.

Nearby sites may share environmental conditions, so site records can be dependent even though each row represents a different site. This can affect the usual uncertainty estimates. Rainfall and other environmental conditions can covary with elevation. These observational data describe modern sampled sites and cannot isolate a causal mechanism or establish the growing conditions of an archaeological specimen on their own.

4. What causal or archaeological inference does this correlation **not** establish?
